Mechanical Hearts saving lives under COVID

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
A strange impact of COVID in the last 18 months is that it’s stopped the possibilities of heart transplants, there used to be 40 a year. There are no ventilators available to keeping brain-dead people alive to harvest their organs when living COVID patients desperately need to be intubated. So, the pendulum has swung back to develop more effective mechanical hearts. With WiTricity and Nano battery technology gaining momentum, they anticipate that in the near future the batteries required to power the LVAD heart mate will be able to be implanted inside the body and charged by a power vest. Currently the batteries are outside the body and charged on the mains.

Summary:
Heart Transplant surgeon Dr Willie Koen says mechanical hearts have many advantages over heart transplants and COVID has impacted the situation further. Heart transplants patients need to be on immunosuppressants and are therefore more vulnerable to developing severe COVID-19 complications. Immunosuppression is not required, however, for implantation of a mechanical heart pump. Transplant patients often die from failing livers and kidneys from long term use of this medication and the transplanted hearts often fail after a few years.

The device replaces the function of the failing heart muscle, pumping the blood around the body to provide vital circulation. The heart acts as a reservoir and the LVAD does the work. Previously, LVADs have mainly served as a temporary option to keep a patient alive until a heart transplant could be performed. Technological advances in VADs have increased the longevity of these devices, increasingly supporting their use as a potential long-term solution for heart failure
While the LVAD component that pumps the blood is implanted within the patient’s chest, it is connected by a driveline, which protrudes through the abdomen, to a controller and battery pack outside the body. The device records clinical data that the treating specialist needs for monitoring the patient’s condition remotely. Currently the LVAD is powered by two external batteries which weigh about 1kg each and are charged by mains electricity lasting about 8 hours at a time. This is a minor inconvenience for people who before the operation they could not walk and talk at the same time.


Further information:
Sadly the 10 year old who had the LVAD exchanged for a heart transplant because as a teenager he didn’t want the inconvenience of the external batteries, died from complications afterwards.

There is a great deal of research at MIT in both Wi Tricity and nano battery development and Dr Koen is confident within the next few years they will be able to implant small batteries into the body which can be charged by wearing a vest at night. Currently the only risk is the drive line which leaves the body to the batteries which can become infected. There is a 79 year old woman who has been living with the device for 10 years now and has no intention of having a transplant.

We have two patients who have had the operation in the last 5 months, both recovering well and discharged from hospital and one patient who is about to have the operation so we can film the process.

Script: A casual stroll in the park with their daughter feels like a dream for Alicia and Johan Van Wyk. Just a few months ago he was at death's door, struggling to breath, never mind walk, and the bag he carries - is literally keeping him alive. Their nightmare began 10 years ago, when as a young fit 28, year old Johan’s heart began to fail
Johan: It was a big shock, the question is going through your mind, why what where
Alicia: Having a six month old baby, the only thing that went through my mind was I'm going to raise her alone at that stage wasn't any hope
Script: The next 10 years of their lives have been a roller coaster - and it's hard to reflect the trauma they have endured. Johan suffered two strokes, organ failure, blood clots, had a pacemaker implanted, and was spending more time in hospital than out. Then earlier this year it looked like the end of the road.
Alicia: I came home for lunch, and when I stopped here, they told me, no, I need to go back there. But by then he was already in a seduced coma his organs were failing.
Derek: Do you think it could be the end?
Alicia: to be quite honest with you. Yes. The doctor at that time also told me, sorry, I don't think there's anything we can do for you. So me being me, I just said there is no giving up.
Script: Putting on a brave face for their child and each other, they prayed for a miracle. Collin Watermeyer was just 36 years old with a young 2 year son
Collin: When I was diagnosed, my son, I tried to pick him up as usual, but that morning I just couldn't, I was weak. And after trying to pick him up, I was out of breath, and so I thought something is wrong with my lungs.
Script: After three weeks in hospital, he was finally diagnosed.
Collin my heart was severely swollen - so ja it was a pretty emotional moment for me in my wife.
Script: For 9 years Collin struggled on, then last year he contracted COVID and started having seizures, a pacemaker was implanted but his health didn’t improve
Derek: You must have wondered if you were going to see your wife and kids again.
Collin, it's scary: I must say Derek….. the pacemaker for me has triggered the reality of my mortality. You know, every time I feel it, ….in my heart , it would remind me, you know, we are mortal beings and we need to savour every moment that we have
Link” In poetry and literature, the heart has been as the window to the soul, the universal language of love and connection. But for these men’s families that’s taken on a whole new scientific dimension.
Script: Both Johan and Collin were in end stage heart failure, their only hope was an artificial heart. World renowned cardiac and transplant surgeon Dr Willie Koen, pioneered ventricular assist device implants in South Africa, and heads up the only unit in the country able to do this world class surgery.
Koen The heart has to pump strongly like this, it’s easy to demonstrate with my hand, and if a person has heart failure, it only pumps like this and when it gets critical it only does this hardly contract anymore and you need six liters of blood per minute to stay alive or to have a good quality of life,
Derek: Now this is the pump and that gets implanted into the chest .
Koen: So it will go into the into the tip of the heart and it will suck all the blood out. This is the actual pump itself and then the blood gets pumped out, through this pipe and this pipe, we connect onto the aorta …. as if the heart was doing it. And the only part that leaves the body is this cable that connects the patient to the actual electricity.
Link “Our heartbeat is something that we largely unaware of except of course when we exercise with our fitness watches, so it is quite a thing to get your head around when that driving force is actually attached to the outside of your body.
Script: The drive line leaves the body through an open wound which requires dressing every 2nd day and a little computer measures the blood flow and the status of the batteries. The heart is driven by two batteries which require charging roughly every 7 hours
Derek: But it must be an uneasy feeling that your life, to some extent, depends on the electricity grid.
Collin: Yeah, it does,the electricity situation in our country is not very encouraging as well, but I have backup batteries that I have and I have to keep charged but when I do do have a lot of physical activity, it consumes a lot of the battery power
Derek: And what's it like being so dependent on all these devices, Johan?
Johan: , this actually is a little bit scary, but yeah,
Derek You get used to it
Derek: A very real situation and we're not being dramatic, but there is load sitting in your area in five minutes time, how will that affect you? What do you have to do
Johan: We've got we have to make sure you have a charged unit. But I bought myself an inverting system, and that's my backup
Derek: What is quite critical is when you change batteries because you've only got a few seconds,
Johan: you're got 12 seconds
Script: And the weirdest thing is they don’t have a pulse or regular heartbeat

Script: There is a special bond between these two young fathers. Johan had his operation in June and Collin in August - they have stayed in touch, comparing notes on their recovery
UPsound on the whatsapp call Collin I know people think this thing was a walk in the park but it wasn’t
Johan?
Collin: He was like the pioneer because he got it first. Seeing him coming to my ward visiting me at that stage, I was also very weak and he told me that the way I am, he was maybe three times worse, and he can now walk, he couldn't do things he couldn’t before. So that gave me a lot of hope.

Script: The new magnetically levitated rotor reduces the risk of blood clots and can last far longer - up to 10 years. Under COVID, heart transplants became impossible, because there were no ventilators available to keep organ donors alive, and the immune suppressants, required for a heart transplant, increased their risk of contracting the virus. But even before the pandemic, there weren’t enough donors for the number of heart transplants required.
Koen: they started developing mechanical pumps long before our transplant research was started. They started this already in the 50s, but the machines were about as big as this room.. And then there was another group of people who started looking into heart transplant. Prof. Chris Barnard and that whole group and eventually the heart transplants won, and then the whole world just went down the heart transplant lane. Buthe mechanical people continued. At the moment, they implanting three times as many artificial pumps in the world than heart transplants.
Derek: Collin if you were offered a transplant now, would you take it?
Collin: I would like to put that off for as long as I can, ….when I get to transplanted heart, I will have to get on immunosuppressive drugs. And in this COVID era, for me, it's too risky……. because with the LVAD I don't need to do that, yes
Alicia:Obviously, this is a temporary thing. 02:32:58:14 if a heart should come around he could go for a heart transplant, 'll worry about that then, for now I'm just savouring the moment
Script: One major drawback is you can’t swim and showering is only possible if the batteries and computer are protected in this special bag, but both Collin and Johan say it’s a small price to pay, to have their lives back
Link The technology when it comes to mechanical hearts is advancing all the time and the vision for the future is that eventually the pump and the battery will be implanted into the body and the battery charged wirelessly
Script: But for now the relief of sending these young fathers home to their families is enough for Dr Koen
Koen Everyone is holding their breaths because they are so many little hurdles till he leaves the hospital. And then when that patient walks into the office a week later, and you see the smiles on the family on the team,then you feel good.
Script: For the first time in 5 years Collin can play with his kids
Collin: I feel I have a zest for life. Now I can actually plan for the future because I see myself in it unlike before I'm healthy, I can work, I can even babysit properly, because in the past, you know, my wife couldn't really leave me with the kids because we didn't know what might happen, the changes have been phenomenal, really.
Script: And Johan can finally take a walk
Johan: it gives you your life back, and courage in life, you can go back to normal, you can walk around everyday without being out of breath. It’s depressing not to be able to do the things you want to do because you don't have the energy
Alicia: We can make plans again, and plan holidays again, that sort of thing because before you couldn't, so I think for us it’s a chance to live
